Poster · iHEALTH Annual Workshop 2026

Medical LLM Grounded in Neuro-Fuzzy VASARI Inference for Interpretable Glioma Characterization in MRI

A framework that characterizes gliomas in MRI in the terminology of the radiologist, where radiomic features become VASARI descriptors through a few fuzzy IF–THEN rules and a medical language model describes the case from those findings and rules.

Across four VASARI descriptors of tumor composition (F4, F5, F6, F14), with a mean macro F1 of 67.32%.

1

Why this study

Gliomas are the most frequent primary tumors of the central nervous system and carry a poor prognosis, and their early characterization improves treatment planning and follow-up. The radiologist describes the tumor in MRI with semantic descriptors, such as the quality of enhancement or the proportion of edema, although the heterogeneity of the tumor hinders an objective and reproducible assessment.

VASARI standardizes that description in a controlled vocabulary of 25 descriptors for gliomas in MRI, while radiomics measures intensity, shape and texture as numerical values without an immediate clinical meaning. This work connects both sides with fuzzy IF–THEN rules that map a few radiomic features onto VASARI categories, so that the information derived from the image is expressed in the standardized terminology of the radiologist, and a medical language model writes a short description from those results as an exploratory output.

2

Method in three stages

aAutomatic segmentation

A 3D Attention U-Net reads the T1, T1ce, T2 and FLAIR volumes and outlines the necrotic core (NCR), the enhancing tumor (ET) and the peritumoral edema (ED).

Data

BraTS 2021: 1,251 adult glioma patients, 983 after excluding cases without the three subregions. The four descriptors share a cohort of 579 training, 193 validation and 194 test patients.

bExplainable characterization

From each subregion, 107 radiomic features are extracted on T1ce with PyRadiomics. A decision tree keeps between two and six of them per descriptor, and a SONFIS model learns one to three IF–THEN rules that predict the VASARI category.

Training targets

VASARI-auto, which derives the descriptors from the segmentation masks without manual annotation.

cDescription with MedGemma

MedGemma (4.3 billion parameters, 4-bit quantized) runs locally with Ollama at temperature 0.2 and is called twice. The first paragraph puts into words seven descriptors taken from VASARI-auto, such as location, side and margin thickness. The second explains F4, F5, F6 and F14 from the SONFIS prediction and its most influential rule.

Status

Exploratory output, outside the evaluated scope.

3

One case, end to end

Segmentation

Ground truth, prediction and error map side by side. The segmentation is good for this patient, with Dice of 92.25%, 94.88% and 92.79% for NCR, ED and ET. False positives are orange and false negatives green.

Rule activation

For enhancement quality, the patient's three feature values are placed on the membership functions of each rule. Rule 1 fires at α = 0.997 and Rule 2 at α = 0.003.

Ground truth: MarkedPredicted: Marked

Generated description

F4, F6 and F14 agree with VASARI-auto. F5 is predicted as 34–67% where VASARI-auto gives 6–33%, with a probability of 0.601. The miss lands in the neighboring category, and the text flags it.

F5: 34–67% vs 6–33%

Against six reference classifiers trained on the same features, SONFIS had the highest mean macro F1 (67.32% against 66.07% for Random Forest). The gap is 1.25 points on a single split, without a significance test.

5

Limitations

Labels come from a tool

The VASARI targets are produced by VASARI-auto and not by radiologists. The rules approximate how that tool generates the descriptors, not expert reasoning.

Four of 25 descriptors

VASARI-auto infers 11 of the 25 descriptors and SONFIS models the four tied to tumor composition. Location, spread and involvement of nearby structures are not modeled.

No quality check on the mask

Training used reference masks and testing used predicted ones. A poor segmentation carries over as a wrong but confident prediction, as one test case showed.

Text is exploratory

The description is a proof of concept, without clinical validation or a check of factual fidelity. A language model can add statements that its input does not support.
